conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Sarah; I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the practice. I spend my days talking with new mothers just like you—checking in on how things are going emotionally in these first weeks and months after baby arrives.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the EPDS). It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us get a snapshot of how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There’s no pass or fail—just honest answers that will guide us in figuring out what kind of support, if any, might be helpful for you right now.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or someone else’s; in that case we’d talk together about the next steps. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification any time.

I’ll read each question aloud and then jot down the number that best matches what you’ve been experiencing. Ready to start?

**Question 1:** Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?  
(0 = as much as I always could, 1 = not quite so much, 2 = definitely not so much, 3 = not at all)

[soft half-smile, eyes a little tired]  
I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a silly joke—but it doesn’t feel as easy or natural as it used to. I’d say… not quite so much.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say… not quite so much.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs quietly, shifts in the chair]

Most things feel... flat. I still get a little spark when my mom brings over my favorite coffee, but it's nothing like before. I guess I'd say... definitely not so much.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to hands, voice small]

Yeah... like when the baby wouldn't settle last night, I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I'm not feeding him right, or I'm missing some cue. It pops into my head several times a day. So, yes... quite a lot.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping my cardigan tighter]

Most of the time. Even when everything’s quiet I’ll suddenly think the baby’s stopped breathing, or I’ll replay tiny things—like whether I buckled the car seat right—over and over. So... yes, very often.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—maybe once or twice this week—it hits out of nowhere. My heart races and I get this wave of “something awful is about to happen,” even when the baby’s fine and the room is calm. So, yes... sometimes.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly, rubbing my temples]

A lot of the time. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, there’s another diaper, another outfit change, another worry. I can manage, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water. So... yes, most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down, voice low]

Yeah… I lie there after the night feed, exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—mostly about the baby, did I burp him enough, is he breathing. It takes me maybe an hour to fall back asleep, and then I wake again with the same loop. So, yes—most nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet, eyes glassy]

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me through the day, even when I’m holding the baby or talking with my mom. I still smile for pictures, but inside it feels heavy. So… yes, most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallowing hard, voice shaky]

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after I couldn’t get him to latch—nothing huge, but I just sat in the glider with tears rolling down. So, yes—sometimes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[hesitates, fingers tightening around the sleeve of my cardigan]

I—I’ve had a couple of quick flashes, like “what if I just kept driving past the house” or “maybe everyone would be better off without me,” but they’re gone as fast as they come. I haven’t thought about how I’d do it or anything… just those little passing thoughts. So… yes, sometimes.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has dulled into a constant gray cloud: laughter is harder to find, days feel overwhelmingly heavy, and anxious thoughts about your baby's safety loop through your mind even at 3 a.m. Although you're still showing up for every diaper change and feeding, you're doing so while battling frequent self-blame, sudden panicky surges, and tearful moments that leave you wondering whether everyone might be better off without you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Her description of things feeling "flat" and "definitely not so much" enjoyment aligns with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "several times a day" and gives a specific example of feeling at fault for baby's distress, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about infant safety and repetitive rumination, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks "once or twice" in the week, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm while still managing tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty returning to sleep due to racing anxious thoughts, occurring "most nights this week," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "most of the time" and describes persistent sadness with metaphors of a "gray cloud" and "heavy" feelings, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorses "yes, sometimes" and describes fleeting passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the 14-point threshold that flags probable major postpartum depression; item 10 scored 2, indicating occasional passive suicidal ideation, which mandates immediate safety evaluation. Your description of feeling <quote>flat</quote>, <quote>most of the time miserable</quote>, near-daily difficulty returning to sleep, recurrent panic symptoms, and multiple daily self-critical thoughts aligns with core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and likely comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review mood and safety plan
2. Request immediate referral to a perinatal mental-health specialist for evaluation of <med>postpartum depression</med> and possible <med>medication</med> or therapy options
3. Involve a trusted adult who can stay with you and the baby until professional support is in place
4. Create a 24-hour safety plan: keep national suicide hotline numbers in your phone and agree to call 911 or go to the nearest <med>emergency department</med> if thoughts of self-harm intensify
5. Schedule brief daily check-ins with a support person to monitor mood, sleep hours, and appetite changes
6. Begin small self-care steps: five-minute outdoor walks, balanced snacks every three hours, and limiting evening screen time to encourage rest
7. Bring this completed EPDS form to your provider so they can track progress and adjust treatment as needed
8. Consider joining a local or online <med>postpartum support group</med> to reduce isolation and learn coping strategies from other mothers
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**  
*(Patient is ~1-week postpartum; responses to EPDS-based interview)*

**Key Findings:**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Pronounced guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Near-daily, intrusive anxious worries and occasional panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily infant tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation without plan or intent (Q10)

**Pattern:** Consistent endorsement of depressive and anxiety symptoms; functional impairment evident; safety concern flagged owing to presence of any self-harm thoughts.

**Screening Impression:**  
High clinical likelihood of postpartum major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; active safety risk requires immediate follow-up (further risk assessment, possible crisis-planning, and referral to specialty perinatal mental health services).
